pages.text:
I was at Jonah’s door at 1:55, wearing the sneakers with the double-knot, which were the only ones in the house that looked like they had a job to do. The door opened before I knocked. Jonah stood there in his helmet, holding his laminated itinerary with both hands, staring at me with the intensity of a kid waiting for test results. Then he looked at my shoes. Then back at my face.

"You came," he said. His voice was quiet, stripped of its usual bounce, sounding like he was checking if the water was hot before stepping in.

"I'm here for all of it," I said. "Even the part about the raft."

Jonah blinked and looked down at the plastic sheet in his hands. He read the first line. "Creek. Raft. Potential for dignity loss." He looked up. "I have never been so confident in a plan that ends in potential."

"I don't care about the plan," I said. "I care about the creek."

He stepped aside. The hallway smelled like bicycle grease and old juice boxes. I walked in, ignoring the clock on the wall because it wasn't his clock, and I had learned not to trust clocks that didn't belong to grandmothers.
pages.image: Max in a red hoodie and messy hair stands in a doorway, while Jonah in a bike helmet holds a laminated sheet, both looking at wet sneakers on the floor; warm indoor light.

pages.text:
The raft was a piece of cardboard wrapped in trash bags. It floated for four seconds in eight inches of water. Then it folded. We were in the creek up to our knees, cold and shivering, but we were laughing so hard my ribs hurt. It was the kind of laugh that comes out of your belly and leaves without asking permission.

Jonah lifted his helmet. Creek water poured out of it in a steady stream. He tipped his head back and let it run down his face, a royal ceremony of wetness. He looked at me, dripping, and smiled.

"You're my best friend," I said. I didn't wait for a reason. I didn't check the schedule. I just said it.

Jonah wiped his face with his sleeve. He pointed at me with his wet finger. "I know," he said. "It's on the laminate."

I tried to argue, but the water was too cold and the joke was too perfect. I just pointed back at him. The creek flowed around our legs, carrying off a single red Lego brick I had dropped. It was gone. I didn't mind.
pages.image: Max and Jonah stand knee-deep in a shallow creek, both in red hoodies or shirts, laughing as water pours from Jonah's helmet; green reeds around them, bright daylight.

pages.text:
Putt-Putt Palace was empty when we arrived. The sky turned the color of a bruised plum in about ten minutes. The first drop hit my nose. Then the sky opened up. The plastic windmill on the last hole spun wildly, a grey fan in a storm.

We did not leave. We stood in the rain, holding our plastic clubs, watching the storm. I put the ball on the tee. I hit it. It went three feet. Then I took another swing, just to see what would happen. The ball flew, wild and high, and sank into the hole on the other side of the green.

A hole-in-one. In a thunderstorm. On a Saturday that had never once rained.

We screamed. We screamed until our voices were hoarse and the rain was soaking through our shirts. Nobody else was there to hear it. The course was just us and the wind and the spinning plastic. I didn't care about the score. I didn't care about the rain. I cared that we were screaming together.
pages.image: Max and Jonah stand in a heavy rainstorm on a minigolf course, arms raised in the air, a small plastic windmill spinning in the background; dark clouds above.

pages.text:
Scoops was closed. The sign in the window said OUT OF POWER. Jonah stared at it for exactly three seconds. I counted. One, two, three. Then he lifted his arms high above his head.

"Rain ice cream!" he shouted.

We walked out into the parking lot where the rain was coming down in thick, heavy sheets. We stood there with our mouths open, letting the drops hit our tongues. It tasted like metal and summer. Five minutes later, Jonah's mom found us. She looked at our soaked hair and our crazy faces. She did not ask questions. She just opened the car door.

In the back seat, Jonah pulled a plastic bag from under his seat. Inside were two old walkie-talkies, the kind with the long antennas that looked like they had survived a war.

"Range is two miles," he said, handing me one. "So it's basically useless. Take it."

I took it. It was heavy, and it was real, and it was finally mine.
pages.image: Max and Jonah sit in the back seat of a car, holding old walkie-talkies, rain dripping from their hair; Jonah smiles, Max looks surprised; interior lit by car dashboard.

pages.text:
We sat on the porch as the rain slowed into a soft mist, and Jonah fidgeted with the strap of his helmet. He looked at me, then down at the walkie-talkie in my hand.

"Is it fixed?" he asked, nodding toward the sky. "The Saturday thing?"

I watched a drop of water roll off the edge of the wet wood and hit the ground, then looked at my shoes. I thought about the clock in the hall, and I thought about the seventy-seven scratches I had made on the closet wall with a pencil.

"I stopped needing it fixed," I said, and my voice sounded like it belonged to someone else, someone who was tired of being the only one who knew the score.

Jonah nodded slowly. He didn't ask why. He just sat there with me, like he understood a joke I hadn't told yet. The rain stopped completely, and the air started to smell like wet dust and pine, which is what my room smells like after I’ve been crying in it for an hour and then cleaned up.

"Okay," Jonah said, breaking the quiet. "New rule. Saturdays. 6:47 a.m. Every week. One of us calls the other."

"You won't remember agreeing to this," I said, because I knew the way his brain worked.

Jonah grinned, a huge, confident smile that took up his whole face. He pulled a pen from his pocket and tapped it against his chin. "Then write it on a laminate."
pages.image: Max and Jonah sit on a wooden porch steps after the rain, holding walkie-talkies, looking at each other; a green Buick visible in the driveway behind them; dusk light.
